text: Stones are in a row, each with a value. Alice and Bob alternate, Alice first. On a turn you take one, two, or three stones from the front. Both play optimally to maximize their own score. Return Alice, Bob, or Tie.

Thanks. Before I dive in, I'd like to clarify a few things. Just to make sure I'm understanding this correctly — you always take from the front, so what's left is a suffix, values can be negative, and I compare the two final scores?
Right — from the front, values from negative one thousand to one thousand, and up to fifty thousand stones.
Let me run through an example. One, two, three, seven: whatever Alice grabs up front, Bob can end up taking the seven. Optimally Alice trails by one, so the answer is Bob.

Hmm, let me think about this for a second. A naive approach would simulate both players and branch three ways on every turn, which is exponential. This problem reminds me of a minimax game DP, and the clean trick is to track a relative score. Let dp of i be the best score difference the current player can achieve starting at stone i. Since what remains is always a suffix, one dimension suffices. After I take some stones for a sum, take, my opponent plays from i plus j plus one and achieves dp of i plus j plus one — which is their lead over me, so I subtract it.

Here's the plan. One: set dp of n to zero — no stones, no difference. Two: go from the last stone back to the first, and try taking one, two, or three stones, keeping a running sum. Three: dp of i is the max of take minus dp of the next index; at the end, positive means Alice, negative means Bob, zero means Tie. One thing worth flagging — the minus is the whole idea: I maximize what I take minus how far the opponent can then pull ahead. And I fill back to front because dp of i needs the next three entries. Does this approach sound good, or would you rather I think of another way?
Sounds good. Code it, and the constant-space version.

The array DP starts every entry at INT_MIN, sets dp of n to zero, and sweeps back to front; the inner loop grows take one stone at a time and keeps the best take minus the opponent's dp. And the constant-space version: dp of i only needs the next three, so I keep three variables and slide the window forward after each stone. Both are linear time. One thing worth flagging — out of range, past the end, counts as zero, matching dp of n equals zero. That's why the three variables can start at zero.

Let's dry-run on one, two, three, seven. The row that matters is stone zero. Alice's best is taking one, two, three for six, minus dp of three, which is seven, so negative one: she grabs six but leaves the seven, and Bob's future lead of seven flips it. So dp of zero is negative one, and the answer is Bob. That matches. As a negative check, with one, two, three, negative nine, Alice dumps the negative nine on Bob: six minus negative nine is fifteen, so Alice wins. Corner case: one, two, three, six is a Tie.

Let me think about complexity here. Time is linear, and space is linear or constant. Oh, one more thing — the reusable idea is: track the relative score and subtract the opponent's optimum. The same trick powers the games where you take from both ends; there the remaining part is an interval from i to j, and the DP becomes two-dimensional. And because stones can be negative, taking more isn't always better — the max handles that automatically.

Nicely done. Three things stood out. You collapsed two players into one relative-score array and explained the minus as handing the turn over. You filled back to front for the dependency and reduced to constant space. And you connected it to the two-ended interval games and the negative-values subtlety. Good work.
